title: Investigation of the health effects of regular pulse consumption
summary:
The TILL study is part of the EatLegu project, which is funded by the Federal Ministry of Agriculture, Food and Regional Identity (BMLEH) as part of the Protein Crop Strategy. The TILL trial aims to investigate the health effects of regular pulse consumption. Specifically, it seeks to determine whether the consumption of novel pulse-based foods (e.g. pasta, bread, snacks made from pulse flour) elicits positive health effects, particularly on fat metabolism, sugar metabolism, and satiety, which are comparable to the consumption of dishes made from whole, minimally processed pulses (e.g. chickpea curry, bean soup, hummus).
Pulses are considered beneficial to health due to their valuable nutrients and their ability to promote long-lasting satiety. Some studies suggest that including pulses in the diet may help prevent or mitigate diseases such as high blood pressure, lipid metabolism disorders, and type 2 diabetes mellitus. For this reason, health organizations in many countries, including Germany, recommend regular consumption of pulses. However, average intake in Germany remains well below general dietary recommendations and therefore should be increased. To achieve this, it seems to be essential to improve consumer acceptance of pulses. A growing number of pulse-based products is now available in supermarkets. These products may help to increase pulse consumption among the population, as they are easy to access and often ready-to-eat or quick to prepare. However, there is still limited evidence as to whether pulses in such processed forms are equally suitable for a healthy diet.
The study will be conducted with 90 overweight participants (Body Mass Index ≥ 25 kg/m²) with an increased waist circumference (≥ 94 cm for men, ≥ 80 cm for women). Participants will be randomly assigned to one of three intervention groups. Participants will consume either at least 130 grams of pulses per day (1) included in dishes as whole pulsesin dishes which are prepared using standard household methods, or (2) in the form of pulse-based foods, or (3) no pulses at all (control group). Participants will be provided with meal plans, recipes and all necessary food items tailored to their individual energy needs. All meals will be prepared at home by the participants themselves. Before and after the four-week intervention period, blood and urine samples will be collected to detect any changes in metabolism that may be associated with increased pulse consumption. In addition, stool samples will be analyzed to determine whether and how the consumed pulses or pulse-based products affect the composition and function of gut bacteria as well as the integrity of the gut barrier.
The results of the TILL study aim to expand current knowledge about the potential health benefits of these new pulse-based foods. This will enable us to assess to which extent these foods could contribute to increasing pulse consumption among the population. The gain in knowledge may finally help to derive appropriate dietary recommendations for consumers.
conditions: Metabolic status in overweight adults (lipid and carbohydrate metabolism)

interventions.name: Diet including traditionally prepared dishes made from whole pulses (at least 130 g pulses/day; daily for 4 weeks). These are processed using standard household methods (e.g., chickpea curry, bean soup, hummus); at least 130 g pulses/day, 4 weeks after a 2-week run-in phase of pulses abstinence

Diet including at least 130 g pulses/day, daily for 4 weeks in a more processed form (e.g., pulse flour). This includes commercially available pulse-based products (e.g., pasta, bread, snacks), as well as home-prepared dishes for example made with pulse flour (e.g., pancakes made from chickpea flour
Diet without pulses (control group), for 4 weeks after a 2-week run-in phase of pulses abstinence

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
- Women and men
- BMI ≥ 25 kg/m²
- Waist circumference ≥ 94 cm for men, ≥ 80 for women 
- Volunteers who are able to comply with the study requirements
- Parameters of liver and kidney function without pathological significance
- Normal thyroid function or euthyroid status in treated thyroid disorders
- Non-smokers
- Omnivorous diet (mixed eater)
- Written informed consent to participate in the study
Exclusion criteria:
- Diseases affecting absorption, digestion, metabolism, or excretion of nutrients
- Diabetes mellitus 
- Acute or chronic infectious diseases
- Tumors requiring therapy
- History of bariatric surgery
- History of gastrointestinal tract surgery affecting absorption, digestion, metabolism, or excretion of nutrients
- History of pancreas surgery
- History of cholecystectomy
- Intake of cholesterol-lowering medication 
- Acute/regular intake of medication resulting in energy or nutrient malabsorption 
- Allergy/intolerance to any food or food components of the dietary intervention
- Use of antibiotics < 10 weeks prior to study entry
- Blood donation during or < 2 weeks prior to study entry
- Pregnancy or breastfeeding 
- Drug, alcohol, or drug abuse 
- Participation in other clinical trials that may effect the outcome of this study
- Individuals living in a care facility
- Individuals deprived of their liberty by court or administrative order
- Individuals who are not expected to comply with study requirements
